svg.aria-label: Diagram: how an Azure Policy initiative groups up to 1000 policy definitions behind a single assignment, and how the compliance percentage that assignment reports is produced, showing resources in scope narrowed by applicability, a compliance state recorded per resource per policy, the rank order used to roll those states up to one state per resource, and the documented percentage formula in which exempt, unknown and protected resources sit in the numerator alongside compliant ones
svg.title: An initiative is one assignment over many rules; the compliance percentage it reports counts exempt, unknown and protected resources on the same side as compliant ones
svg.text: An initiative saves assignments. The percentage it reports is a different question.
Grouping rules is an arithmetic decision about a hard limit. Reading the resulting number requires knowing which resources were counted.
Initiative definition — one object, many rules
A group of existing definitions, worked with as a single item.
policyDefinitions[] — up to 1000 policy definitions
policyDefinitionReferenceId — what overrides and groups target
definitionVersion — per member, unset takes the latest major
parameters — up to 400, passed down into member definitions
Initiative-level parameters cannot be altered once assigned.
Set a defaultValue when defining them; a change means a new assignment.
A member definition still holds at most 20 parameters of its own.
One assignment instead of many — the actual reason
The per-scope budgets are asymmetric, and one of them binds first.
Policy definitions per scope — 500
Initiative definitions per scope — 200, and 2,500 per tenant
Policy or initiative assignments per scope — 200
1000 rules assigned one by one is five times the assignment limit.
The same 1000 inside one initiative consume a single assignment.
The cost: one scope, one enforcementMode, one identity, one set of
exclusions for every rule in the group.
Where the number comes from — four steps, and the first one removes resources from the denominator
Resources in scope
Every child container and
resource under the
assignment scope
Applicable?
type, name and kind · mode
notScopes · resourceSelectors
exemptions
One state per pair
Compliance state is decided
per resource, per policy
assignment
Rolled up by rank
Scope, initiative, control,
policy or resource — the
highest rank present wins
Applicability is not compliance. A resource ruled inapplicable is not assessed at all, so it never appears in the numbers either way.
Rank order: non-compliant, then compliant, then error, conflicting, protected, exempted, unknown. Not started and not registered do not roll up.
The documented compliance percentage
overall compliance % = (compliant + exempt + unknown + protected)
/ (compliant + exempt + unknown + non-compliant + conflicting + error + protected)
Exempt, unknown and protected sit in the numerator. Granting an exemption raises the score; so does an unattested manual policy.
Two rollup consequences worth knowing before quoting the number to anyone
A resource non-compliant to one policy in an initiative is non-compliant for the whole initiative, whatever the other 999 say.
A resource shows as exempt for an initiative only if it is exempt from, or unknown to, every applicable policy in it — compliant outranks exempt.
A high percentage is not evidence that anything is being enforced.
An assignment in DoNotEnforce reports compliance and blocks nothing. Excluded scopes are not evaluated and not counted at all. A rule whose
type condition matches nothing in the estate is applicable to no resource, and a policy with no applicable resources cannot lower any score.
Sources: initiative definition structure, compliance states, applicability logic and Azure subscription and service limits, on Microsoft Learn.
